Samantha — thanks for the clear notes and the sketch. Below is a concise summary you can share with security / procurement. I copied Ben (serving/runtime) and Laura (customer ops) for the operational handoff details.

Summary answers (Dedicated capacity vs Private VPC):

1) Tenant separation and data at rest
- Dedicated capacity: customer workloads run on reserved GPU pools with strict tenant isolation at the hypervisor and orchestration layer. No customer model artifacts or KV caches from Dedicated instances are shared across tenants; ephemeral KV caches are stored in memory on the worker and are not persisted to shared network storage.
- Private VPC: customer manages networking and has a private control plane option; data plane (model weights, caches) remains inside your VPC / on-prem infrastructure per the deployment agreement. Redwood's hosted control plane can optionally retain only minimal operational metadata required for billing/faulting (see retention section).

2) Control plane metadata and retention
- For Private VPC deployments with private control plane enabled, Redwood does not retain raw request payloads or model outputs. We retain service-level telemetry (timestamps, request size, error codes) for troubleshooting; retention period is configurable in the enterprise contract (default 30 days).
- For Dedicated customers on Redwood-managed infrastructure, we retain request-level logs for 7 days by default; longer retention can be negotiated. Request logs can be redacted to exclude model outputs if that is required for PHI constraints.

3) Ops handoff (runtime updates / kernel/quantization changes)
- Dedicated (Redwood-managed): Redwood applies serving runtime patches and kernel updates according to our maintenance windows with notification. We offer a canary rollout per pool and a rollback path.
- Private VPC (customer-managed nodes): customer ops apply runtime updates; Redwood provides release notes, container images, and a recommended upgrade checklist. Redwood can also run upgrades as a managed service under an ops agreement.

Attachments: I attached a short one-pager comparing the deployment modes (redwood-deployment-comparison-onepager.pdf) and noted the parts you should push to Procurement.

Next steps / asks:
- Samantha: confirm whether Brightline requires absolute zero retention of request-level logs (we can propose a redaction policy and DocuSign amendment).
- Marco: if you can mark which network segments in your sketch are public vs private, Laura can draft an ops runbook.
- We'll prepare a short contract addendum template for "no model-output retention" if that is the direction.

Thanks — happy to jump on a quick 20-min call with security if helpful.

Samantha — quick technical clarifications from runtime/serving: 

- Ephemeral KV caches: they are purely in-memory on the GPU worker process. No on-disk persistence on shared filesystems by default. In Dedicated, we also provide an option to mount customer-managed encrypted volumes if you want replication to an external store (not recommended for PHI unless you control encryption keys).
- Model artifacts: model weights are loaded into worker memory; if you use Redwood-managed model hosting we keep a single copy of the model binary per pool; access controls prevent cross-tenant reads. In Private VPC you can request that model binaries are pulled from a customer-controlled artifact registry.
- Sidecar metadata: small indexing metadata (request ids, trace ids) are emitted to the tracing pipeline. We can suppress trace payloads and limit retention to 0 days on contract.

Operational note: If Brightline needs "no retention" for request payloads we typically implement a combination of (1) redaction at ingress, (2) zero-day retention for logs, and (3) an addendum specifying no outputs persist in S3 or equivalent. We can draft language for Procurement.

Happy to do a very short tech drop for your security team — 15 mins to walk the KV lifecycle and how caches are collected/cleared.
